q: An insurance broker's team has approved the design for a Claude-based quote-comparison assistant. Engineers are now writing the service that assembles prompt templates, calling the Messages API with retry logic, and writing unit tests for the template-rendering functions as each module is completed. A separate QA group will later run end-to-end acceptance tests on the full system. Which systems life cycle phase does the engineers' current work belong to?
options: Implementation
Integration and testing
System design
Operations and maintenance
exp: Writing code against an approved design, including unit tests for individual modules as they are built, is Implementation. Integration and testing comes later, when the full assembled system is verified against acceptance criteria, which is the QA group's future end-to-end work. The fact that tests are being written does not by itself make this the testing phase.

q: A health insurer is starting a Claude-powered prior-authorization assistant. Stakeholders disagree about whether the assistant should be allowed to approve requests automatically or only recommend decisions. The team is running workshops to prioritize must-have versus nice-to-have capabilities, documenting regulatory constraints, and agreeing on measurable acceptance criteria. No architecture or model has been chosen. Which phase is this?
options: Requirements analysis
System design
Implementation
Integration and testing
exp: Eliciting and prioritizing what the system must do, capturing constraints, and agreeing on acceptance criteria before any architecture is chosen is Requirements analysis. Deciding between auto-approve and recommend-only is a scope decision, not a design decision.

q: A software company is writing requirements for a Claude-based pull-request assistant. Which TWO of the following statements are functional requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: The assistant shall post a summary comment describing the changes on every newly opened pull request
The assistant shall label a pull request as needs-tests when changed source files have no corresponding test changes
The assistant must remain available 99.5% of the time during business hours in every supported region
The assistant's infrastructure must satisfy the company's SOC 2 Type II security controls
exp: Functional requirements describe behaviors the system performs: posting summaries and applying labels. Availability targets and compliance with security control frameworks are non-functional (quality or constraint) requirements.

q: During an audit of a Claude-powered claims-triage system, regulators ask the team to demonstrate that every approved requirement is addressed by the design and verified by at least one evaluation or test case. Which artifact most directly provides this evidence?
options: A requirements traceability matrix linking each requirement to its design elements and to the eval or test cases that verify it
The project's sprint backlog, showing all user stories that were moved to the done column during development
The production monitoring dashboard, showing request volume, latency percentiles, and error rates over the past quarter
The full Git commit history of the prompt templates, showing every change made to each prompt since the project began
exp: A traceability matrix maps requirements forward to design and verification, and backward from tests to requirements, which proves coverage. Backlogs, dashboards, and commit histories record activity, but none of them shows that each requirement was verified.

q: A bank is retiring a Claude-based document-intake assistant that a new platform has replaced. Which TWO activities belong to the disposal phase of the systems life cycle? (Select TWO.)
options: Revoke the assistant's API keys and delete its workspace credentials so they can no longer be used
Delete documents the assistant stored with the Files API, and archive required records per the retention policy
Rotate the assistant's API keys on a quarterly schedule as part of routine credential hygiene
Migrate the assistant to the latest model snapshot after re-running its evaluation suite
exp: Disposal means decommissioning: revoking access and handling data according to retention rules, which covers deleting what is no longer needed and archiving what must be kept. Routine key rotation and model upgrades are operations and maintenance activities for a system that is still live.

q: A mental-health journaling app calls the Messages API, and some responses render as an empty or truncated message in the UI. The logs show HTTP 200 for these responses with stop_reason "refusal". What is the correct handling?
options: Detect stop_reason refusal explicitly and show a graceful fallback or route the conversation appropriately, rather than resending the same request unchanged
Treat these responses as transient server errors and automatically retry the identical request with exponential backoff until normal text is returned
Raise max_tokens on future requests, since a refusal stop reason indicates the model ran out of budget before finishing its normal answer
Ignore the stop_reason field and render whatever partial text arrived, since an HTTP 200 status guarantees the response is complete and usable
exp: A refusal comes back as a successful (200) response with stop_reason 'refusal'. Applications should check stop_reason and handle refusals deliberately. Retrying the identical request usually gives the same result, and max_tokens has nothing to do with refusals.

q: An inventory agent occasionally receives a response with stop_reason "max_tokens" whose last content block is a tool_use block. Executing that tool call fails because a required field is missing from its input. What should the application do?
options: Treat the truncated tool_use block as incomplete, and retry the request with a higher max_tokens to get a complete tool call
Execute the tool call with default values for the missing fields, since Claude intended to call the tool and the stop is harmless
Send a tool_result with is_error set to true for the truncated call so Claude regenerates only the missing input fields
Switch tool_choice to any for the next request, since forcing a tool call ensures the input is never cut off by max_tokens
exp: If generation hits max_tokens while emitting a tool_use block, the tool input may be incomplete. The documented handling is to retry with a higher max_tokens. Guessing missing values or forcing tools does not fix the truncation.

q: A construction firm's application sends multiple large site-survey PDFs and high-resolution photos as base64 content in a single Messages API request. The request is rejected with HTTP 413 request_too_large before any processing occurs. What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Reduce the request payload below the API's request size limit, for example by uploading the files once with the Files API and referencing their file IDs
Raise max_tokens so the API allocates enough capacity to accept the larger payload, since 413 means output space is insufficient
Switch the request to streaming mode, since streaming requests are exempt from size limits because the content is sent incrementally
Retry the identical request with exponential backoff, since 413 indicates temporary server congestion when handling large uploads
exp: HTTP 413 means the request exceeds the Messages API's maximum request size, which is measured in megabytes. Base64 inflates file size. Uploading the files once through the Files API and referencing their IDs, or sending fewer or smaller files, keeps requests under the limit. max_tokens and streaming do not change request size limits.

q: A fintech company sees a small number of puzzling API errors in production and opens a support ticket with Anthropic. Support asks for information that will let them locate the exact failing requests. What should the team provide, and make a habit of logging?
options: The request-id value from the API response headers of each failing request
The full API key used by the service, so support can search all of its traffic
The SDK version and the operating system of the host that made the requests
The model alias used in the request, so support can filter by that model's traffic
exp: Every API response includes a unique request-id header, and the SDKs also expose it on response objects. Logging it lets Anthropic support find the specific request. Never share API keys, and model or SDK versions do not identify individual requests.

q: A real-estate platform sends Claude listing photos taken at 4000x3000 pixels together with a question, with the question text placed before the images. Responses are slow and image-related answers are sometimes weaker than expected. Which TWO changes follow Anthropic's vision guidance? (Select TWO.)
options: Resize images to within the recommended dimensions before sending, since oversized images add latency without improving quality
Place the images before the question text in the user message, since Claude performs best when images come first
Convert each image to a lengthy text description first, since Claude analyzes text descriptions more accurately than pixels
Increase the image resolution further to 8000x6000 pixels, since higher resolutions always improve Claude's visual accuracy
exp: Images larger than the recommended size are downscaled anyway, which adds latency without improving quality, so resize them beforehand. Anthropic's guidance also notes Claude works best with images placed before the text that asks about them. Converting images to text descriptions throws away visual information.

q: A compliance team wants answers about long policy documents in which every claim can be traced to the exact supporting passage, without engineering their own quote-matching. Which TWO statements about the Citations feature are accurate? (Select TWO.)
options: Enable citations on the document content blocks, and Claude's response text will include citations pointing to the supporting passages
The cited_text returned with each citation does not count toward output tokens, so citations do not add their quoted text to billed output
Citations only work with PDF uploads, so plain-text documents must first be converted to PDF before citations can be enabled
Citations require the model to be forced with tool_choice, so a dedicated citation tool must be defined in the tools array
exp: Citations are enabled per document with citations: {enabled: true}. Responses then contain text blocks with citation objects that reference document locations. The quoted cited_text is not counted toward output tokens. Citations support plain text, PDF, and custom content documents, and no tool is needed.

q: A knowledge-base agent uses a custom search_kb client tool that returns retrieved chunks as one long plain-text string. The team wants Claude's answers to cite the specific retrieved chunks with source attribution, the same way it cites documents. Which change enables this?
options: Return the retrieved chunks from the tool as search_result content blocks, each with a source, title, and content
Append the instruction "always cite your sources" to the tool description so Claude formats inline references itself
Replace the custom tool with the web_search server tool, since only Anthropic-hosted search can produce citations
Store each chunk with the Files API and pass the file IDs in the system prompt so citations attach automatically
exp: Search result content blocks let custom RAG tools (or the user message) supply results with source and title metadata, and Claude can then produce citations that point to them. Prompt instructions produce unverifiable free-form references. Citations are not limited to web search.

q: A research firm submits large Message Batches every weekend. Every request shares a 40,000-token instruction prefix, and an analyst usually downloads results only when preparing a monthly report. Which TWO practices should the team adopt? (Select TWO.)
options: Download batch results promptly, since results remain available only for a limited period (29 days) after the batch is created
Use prompt caching with the 1-hour TTL on the shared prefix, since batch processing can take longer than the 5-minute cache lifetime
Avoid prompt caching in batches entirely, since batch discounts and cache discounts cannot both apply to the same request
Split each batch into separate synchronous calls, since batches cannot include requests that share an identical prefix
exp: Batch results expire after 29 days, so a monthly retrieval can miss them. Caching works with batches and the discounts stack. Because batch requests may run at any point within the processing window, Anthropic suggests the 1-hour cache TTL to improve hit rates on shared prefixes.

q: After a multi-step tool-use exchange, an application wants Claude's final turn to be a plain-text summary with no further tool calls. The developer removes the tools array from that last request, and the API returns a 400 error because the conversation history contains tool_use and tool_result blocks. What is the correct approach?
options: Keep the tools array in the request and set tool_choice to {"type":"none"} so Claude cannot call tools on that turn
Strip every tool_use and tool_result block from the history so the request no longer references any tools at all
Set tool_choice to {"type":"auto"} and add max_tokens of 1 to the tools array so no tool call can be generated
Move the tool definitions from the tools array into the system prompt as text so they no longer count as tools
exp: When the conversation contains tool_use/tool_result blocks, the tool definitions must still be present. tool_choice: none prevents new tool calls while keeping the history valid. Stripping the tool blocks loses context, and the other options are not valid mechanisms.

q: An enterprise agent integrates with dozens of internal systems through roughly 300 tool definitions. The definitions alone consume tens of thousands of tokens on every request, and tool selection accuracy drops as the catalog grows. Which approach is designed for this situation?
options: Use the tool search tool and mark rarely used tools with defer_loading so Claude discovers and loads tool definitions on demand
Set tool_choice to any so Claude is forced to evaluate all 300 tools on every turn instead of skipping over less familiar ones
Shorten every tool description to a single word so the 300 definitions fit in fewer tokens without changing the architecture
Cache the full tool list with a 1-hour TTL, since cached tool definitions do not occupy any space in the model's context window
exp: The tool search tool lets Claude search a large catalog and load only the definitions it needs (deferred tools are marked with defer_loading: true). That saves context and improves selection. Caching reduces cost but cached tokens still occupy the context window. One-word descriptions make selection worse.

q: A finance agent must check expense compliance for 200 employees. Today it calls get_expenses once per employee, and every full result lands in Claude's context, although only a handful of flagged rows matter. The approach is slow and consumes huge amounts of context. Which capability most directly addresses this?
options: Programmatic tool calling, where Claude writes code in the code execution environment that calls the tool and filters results before they reach its context
Parallel tool use alone, since issuing all 200 calls in one turn removes the context cost of the results returned for each employee
Strict tool use, since validating each get_expenses input against the schema shrinks the size of every result returned to the model
Fine-grained tool streaming, since streaming each tool input in pieces prevents large results from accumulating in the context window
exp: Programmatic tool calling lets Claude orchestrate tools from code, with tools opted in via allowed_callers. Loops, aggregation, and filtering happen in the execution environment, so only the final relevant output enters Claude's context, which cuts round trips and token use. Parallel calls still put every result into context.

q: A travel company's book_trip tool has a deeply nested input schema. Calls are structurally valid but often use the wrong conventions: dates as "next Friday" instead of ISO 8601, and airport names instead of IATA codes. Which TWO statements correctly describe the tools available to fix this? (Select TWO.)
options: Adding input_examples to the tool definition shows Claude concrete, correctly formatted calls, which helps with conventions a schema alone cannot convey
Strict tool use guarantees conformance to the schema's structure and types, but it does not by itself teach conventions such as which date format to use
Setting tool_choice to the book_trip tool makes Claude follow the field conventions, since forced calls are validated against example formats
Lowering temperature to zero guarantees ISO dates and IATA codes, since deterministic sampling always selects the canonical value format
exp: Strict mode enforces the schema's structure. Usage conventions (formats, codes, how parameters relate) are best shown with input_examples, plus clear descriptions or enums where possible. Forcing a tool or changing temperature does not teach format conventions.

q: A QA automation agent has a client tool, capture_screenshot, that grabs a PNG of the application under test. The team wants Claude to visually inspect each screenshot after the tool runs. How should the tool's output be returned?
options: Include an image content block (base64 or file reference) inside the tool_result block's content
Return the screenshot's local file path as a text string so Claude can open the file from its own environment
Return the image in the next request's system prompt, since images are not allowed inside tool_result blocks
Encode the PNG as a base64 string in a text block so Claude decodes it and views the image in its reasoning
exp: A tool_result's content can be a list of content blocks, including image blocks, so tools can return visual output for Claude to analyze. Claude cannot open your local file paths, and base64 placed in text is just text.

q: A Python developer wants Claude to call a few plain Python functions as tools. They want the SDK to handle the loop of sending requests, running the requested functions, and returning results until Claude finishes, without adopting the full Claude Agent SDK. Which option fits best?
options: Use the Anthropic SDK's tool runner with functions decorated as tools, which automates the tool-call loop
Use the Message Batches API, which runs all tool calls server-side and returns only the final answer
Use the web_fetch server tool, pointing it at a local endpoint that wraps each Python function
Use structured outputs, since JSON outputs execute matching Python functions automatically
exp: The Anthropic SDKs include a tool runner (in beta) that builds tool schemas from decorated functions and runs the tool-use loop for you. The Agent SDK is a heavier framework for full agents. Batches do not execute client tools, and server tools cannot reach your local functions.

q: A payments team uses structured outputs with a JSON schema whose amount field includes "minimum": 0 and whose reference field includes "maxLength": 20. They are surprised to occasionally see a negative amount after enabling the feature. What is the accurate understanding?
options: Some JSON Schema constraints, such as numeric bounds and string length limits, are not enforced by constrained decoding, so the application must still validate them
Structured outputs never guarantee the output matches the schema's types, so any field can be returned with an unexpected type on any given request
The minimum keyword is enforced only when strict is also set on a tool, so adding strict: true to the request will enforce numeric bounds
Negative numbers indicate the request was routed to a model that does not support structured outputs, so the model ID must be pinned explicitly
exp: Structured outputs guarantee the schema's structure and types, but some constraint keywords, including numeric minimum/maximum and string length limits, are not supported by the constrained decoder. The SDKs can strip them from the schema and validate on the client. Enforce business rules in application code.

q: A tutoring agent with prompt caching enables thinking on some turns and disables it on others within the same conversation. Monitoring shows the system prompt and tool definitions keep hitting the cache, but cache reads of the conversation messages keep failing. What explains this?
options: Changing thinking parameters between requests invalidates cached message content, while system prompt and tool caches remain valid
Thinking blocks can never be cached, so any conversation containing thinking blocks cannot benefit from caching of its messages
The tutoring agent exceeded the maximum of four breakpoints, so the API drops the message-level breakpoint whenever thinking is on
Cached messages expire immediately when thinking is enabled, because thinking requests always use a separate one-minute cache
exp: Changes to thinking settings (enabled or disabled, or the budget) invalidate cache entries for messages. Cached system prompts and tool definitions survive these changes. Keep the thinking configuration stable within a conversation to preserve message cache hits.

q: A news-summary service runs a current model with thinking disabled. A teammate claims the effort parameter is irrelevant because it only controls thinking depth. What is the accurate understanding?
options: Effort still applies with thinking disabled, influencing how many tokens Claude spends on text and tool calls
Effort is rejected with a 400 error unless thinking is enabled, so it must be removed from these requests
Effort only changes the order in which content blocks are returned, not the number of tokens produced
Effort applies only to Batch API requests, so synchronous summary requests ignore the parameter entirely
exp: Effort is a behavioral signal for overall token spend. It affects response thoroughness and tool usage whether or not thinking is enabled. With thinking enabled it also shapes how much Claude thinks.

q: A long-running support conversation uses a single cache_control breakpoint that the application always places on the final message block. After a run of turns that each add many content blocks (tool calls and results), the cache read hits stop even though earlier content is unchanged. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The automatic prefix check only looks back a limited number of blocks from a breakpoint, so add an additional earlier breakpoint to anchor stable content
Cached content expires after 20 turns regardless of TTL, so the application should restart the conversation with a fresh system prompt
Breakpoints on message blocks are ignored once tool results are present, so the breakpoint must move to the system prompt
The cache only stores the most recent user message, so earlier turns must be resent in the system prompt each time
exp: From each breakpoint, the cache checks for prefix hits only within a limited lookback window of about 20 content blocks. If more blocks than that are added between writes, the previous cache entry is not found. Adding an earlier breakpoint, up to four in total, keeps stable content reachable.

q: To improve tool selection, an application reorders its 40 tool definitions on every request so the tools most relevant to the user's query come first. The system prompt is byte-identical and cached, yet cache_read_input_tokens is now always zero. Why?
options: Tools come first in the cached prefix, so reordering them changes the prefix and invalidates the cache for the system prompt and messages that follow
Tool definitions can never be cached, so any request containing tools disables caching for the system prompt as a side effect
Requests with more than 32 tools exceed the cache size limit, so caching is silently disabled for the entire request
The cache only matches when tool_choice is any, so the default auto setting prevents the system prompt from being reused
exp: The cache prefix is built in the order tools, then system, then messages. Any change to the tool definitions, including their order, invalidates everything after them. Keep tools stable, or handle relevance another way, for example with tool search or deferred loading.

q: A team enables server-side compaction for a long-running agent. When the context grows large, the API returns a compaction block summarizing earlier work. The application, however, only stores text blocks when rebuilding the conversation, and after compaction the agent seems to have forgotten its progress. What is the fix?
options: Preserve the compaction block in the assistant content when appending responses to the history, so later requests carry the summary forward
Disable compaction and instead raise max_tokens on each request, since a larger output budget lets the agent retain its earlier progress
Copy the compaction summary into a new system prompt and delete all messages, since compaction blocks cannot be sent back to the API
Send the compaction block as a separate user message wrapped in XML tags, since assistant turns cannot contain compaction content
exp: With server-side compaction, the API returns a compaction block that stands in for the earlier history. The application must keep that block in the conversation, by appending the full response content, so subsequent requests continue from the summary. Dropping it discards the compacted state.

q: An analytics agent's team preloads every potentially relevant table schema, query log, and wiki page into the prompt at the start of each task, using a large share of the context window before any work begins. Following Anthropic's context-engineering guidance, which strategy should they adopt?
options: Just-in-time retrieval: keep lightweight references (table names, file paths, queries) and let the agent load data through tools when needed
Front-loading: add even more reference material up front, since a fuller context window always produces more accurate analytical results
Random sampling: include a random 50% of the reference material on each task so the context stays within a predictable token budget
Compression: base64-encode all reference material so it occupies fewer tokens while still being readable by the model during analysis
exp: Context is a finite resource with diminishing returns. Anthropic's guidance favors just-in-time strategies, where agents hold lightweight identifiers and pull in data at runtime through tools, exploring progressively rather than preloading everything. Base64 increases token counts.

q: A team builds a coding agent that must implement a large application across many sessions, each starting with a fresh context window. Early runs tried to build everything at once, ran out of context mid-feature, and left the next session confused about what was done. Which TWO practices from Anthropic's guidance on long-running agent harnesses address this? (Select TWO.)
options: Maintain a progress file and a structured feature list, and commit to git with descriptive messages so each new session can quickly recover state
Have each session work on one feature at a time and verify it end to end before marking it complete, leaving the codebase in a clean state
Instruct the agent to implement all remaining features in a single session so that no state ever needs to be handed between context windows
Rely on the model to remember earlier sessions' work, since prior context windows are automatically restored when a new session begins
exp: Anthropic's harness guidance uses persistent artifacts (progress notes, a feature list, git history) so fresh sessions can get their bearings, plus incremental work: one feature at a time, tested end to end, leaving a clean state. Nothing carries over between context windows automatically.

q: A publishing house uses Claude to translate literary novels. Clear quality criteria exist (tone, idiom, cultural nuance), and a first draft can be measurably improved when specific critique is fed back. Which workflow pattern fits best?
options: Evaluator-optimizer: one call drafts the translation while another evaluates it against the criteria and returns feedback in a loop
Routing: classify each chapter by genre and direct it to a translation prompt that is specialized for that genre
Parallelization by sectioning: split each chapter into paragraphs and translate all of them independently at once
Orchestrator-workers: a central model dynamically spawns a separate worker for every sentence in the chapter
exp: Evaluator-optimizer fits when there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement adds measurable value. Literary translation is Anthropic's own example. Translating sections independently loses cross-paragraph nuance.

q: A security team wants higher confidence when Claude reviews code for vulnerabilities. They plan to run several different review prompts over the same code and flag the code if any of them finds a problem. Which pattern is this?
options: Parallelization by voting
Prompt chaining
Evaluator-optimizer
Routing
exp: Voting runs the same task several times, or with varied prompts, to get diverse outputs, then aggregates them with a rule such as 'flag if any finds an issue'. Anthropic cites vulnerability review as an example of voting.

q: A marketing team generates long-form articles by first producing an outline, then writing the article from the outline. Some outlines miss required sections, which wastes the expensive writing step. Which design change best applies the prompt-chaining pattern?
options: Add a programmatic gate after the outline step that checks for required sections before the writing step runs
Merge outline and article into one larger prompt so that the model can fix outline mistakes while it writes
Run the writing step on several outlines in parallel and keep whichever article turns out to be the longest
Replace both steps with an autonomous agent that decides on its own whether an outline step is needed at all
exp: Prompt chaining breaks a task into fixed sequential steps and can add programmatic checks ('gates') between them to keep the process on track. Checking the outline before writing is the textbook example.

q: A coding agent repeatedly makes errors with a file-editing tool after it changes directories, because the tool accepts relative paths. According to Anthropic's guidance on designing the agent-computer interface, what is the best fix?
options: Change the tool so it requires absolute file paths, making this class of mistake impossible (poka-yoke the tool)
Add a paragraph to the system prompt reminding the agent to track its current working directory carefully
Remove the file-editing tool and have the agent rewrite files through shell commands so it can see the paths
Increase the model's effort so that it reasons more carefully about relative paths before each edit it makes
exp: Anthropic recommends investing in tool design as carefully as prompts, and changing arguments so mistakes are harder to make ('poka-yoke'). In its SWE-bench agent, requiring absolute paths eliminated relative-path errors.

q: A lead research agent delegates subtasks with short instructions like "research the semiconductor shortage". Subagents duplicate each other's work, leave gaps, and return results in inconsistent formats. Which TWO changes to the delegation does Anthropic's multi-agent research guidance recommend? (Select TWO.)
options: Give each subagent a clear objective, the expected output format, and guidance on which tools and sources to use
Define clear task boundaries for each subagent, and scale the number of subagents and tool calls to the query's complexity
Give every subagent the identical brief instruction so their outputs are consistent and easy to merge afterward
Always spawn the maximum number of subagents for every query so that no aspect of the topic is ever missed
exp: Anthropic found that vague delegation causes duplicated work and gaps. Each subagent needs an objective, output format, tool and source guidance, and clear boundaries. Effort should scale with query complexity rather than always maxing out the number of subagents.

q: A commerce company designs a multi-agent system in which a capable orchestrator plans tasks and many worker subagents perform narrow, well-defined subtasks such as extracting fields from product pages. They want to control cost without sacrificing overall quality. Which TWO choices are sound? (Select TWO.)
options: Use a fast, low-cost model such as Haiku 4.5 for the narrow worker subtasks while a more capable model orchestrates
Validate the model assignment for each role on an evaluation set before rolling it out to production traffic
Use the most capable and expensive model for every worker, since subagent quality never matters if the orchestrator is strong
Assign models to roles based only on public benchmark rankings, so that task-specific evaluation becomes unnecessary
exp: A common pattern pairs a frontier model for planning with fast, inexpensive models such as Haiku for well-scoped subtasks. Model choices should be validated on your own task-specific evals rather than generic benchmarks.

q: A team's Agent SDK application processes a customer's data-migration request in one run. The next day, the customer asks a follow-up question that depends on everything the agent did in that run. How should the application continue with the earlier context?
options: Capture the session ID from the first run and pass it with the resume option so the agent continues that session
Start a new query and paste the final answer from the first run into the prompt, since sessions cannot be continued
Re-run the original prompt from scratch so the agent reproduces the same context before answering the follow-up
Increase max_turns on a new query, since a higher turn limit automatically loads the context of previous runs
exp: The Agent SDK manages sessions. Capture the session ID (it is reported in the init system message and on results) and resume it to continue with the full prior context. Forking is also available for branching. max_turns only limits turns.

q: A team migrates an internal workflow from interactive Claude Code to the Claude Agent SDK. They expect the agent to follow their repository's CLAUDE.md conventions and to behave like Claude Code, but it ignores CLAUDE.md and acts more generically. Which TWO configuration changes address this? (Select TWO.)
options: Set setting_sources to include "project" so the SDK loads project settings and CLAUDE.md from the filesystem
Use the claude_code system prompt preset, since the SDK otherwise uses a minimal system prompt rather than Claude Code's
Rename CLAUDE.md to AGENTS.md, since the Agent SDK reads only AGENTS.md files when it starts a new session
Increase max_turns, since CLAUDE.md is only read after the agent has completed a minimum number of turns
exp: By default the Agent SDK does not load filesystem settings or CLAUDE.md, and it uses a minimal system prompt. To get Claude Code-like behavior, opt in with setting_sources (for example ['project']) and the claude_code system prompt preset, optionally with appended instructions.

q: An Agent SDK agent writes generated reports with the Write tool. Policy requires that every write lands inside a sandbox directory, even when Claude chooses a path elsewhere, and the team prefers redirecting the write over blocking it outright. Which mechanism supports this?
options: A PreToolUse hook or permission callback that returns modified tool input, rewriting the file path into the sandbox before execution
A PostToolUse hook that moves each written file into the sandbox after the Write tool has already created it elsewhere
A system prompt instruction telling Claude to always choose paths inside the sandbox directory for every report it writes
Removing the Write tool from allowed_tools so the agent prints each report to its final text response instead
exp: Hooks and the canUseTool permission callback can allow a call with updated input. Rewriting the path before execution enforces the policy deterministically. A PostToolUse hook acts after the file has already been written outside the sandbox.

q: An engineer wants Claude Code to analyze a large, unfamiliar codebase and propose a step-by-step refactoring approach for review, guaranteeing that no files are modified and no commands run until the plan is approved. What should they use?
options: Plan mode, which lets Claude read and analyze the codebase and present a plan without making changes
Auto-accept edits mode, so Claude applies the refactor quickly and the engineer reviews the git diff later
The --dangerously-skip-permissions flag, so Claude can explore freely without interrupting with prompts
Headless mode with -p, since non-interactive runs are read-only by default and cannot modify any files
exp: Plan mode (cycle to it with Shift+Tab, or start with --permission-mode plan) restricts Claude to read-only analysis and planning until you approve. Headless mode is not read-only by default, and the other options remove safeguards.

q: A team repeatedly types a long prompt asking Claude Code to fetch a GitHub issue, find the relevant code, implement a fix, and write tests. They want to trigger this with something like /fix-issue 1234 and share it with everyone via the repository. What is the right approach?
options: Create a project-level custom command or skill in the repository's .claude/ directory whose prompt uses $ARGUMENTS for the issue number
Add the prompt to each engineer's shell history, and recall it with reverse search whenever an issue needs to be fixed
Put the prompt in .claude/settings.json under a commands key, which Claude Code converts into an executable script
Add the prompt to the global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so Claude automatically runs it at the start of every session
exp: Project-scoped custom slash commands or skills stored in the repository's .claude/ directory are shared through version control and can take arguments via $ARGUMENTS. settings.json does not define prompts, and CLAUDE.md is context, not a command.

q: A team writes a PreToolUse hook script to block Bash commands that touch the production database. When it detects a violation, the script prints a message and exits with code 1, yet the commands still run. Which TWO approaches correctly block the tool call? (Select TWO.)
options: Exit with code 2, which blocks the tool call and feeds the hook's stderr message back to Claude
Return JSON output with a permissionDecision of deny and a reason explaining why the call was blocked
Exit with code 1 but print the message to stdout instead of stderr, so Claude Code detects the violation
Register the same script as a PostToolUse hook instead, since only post-execution hooks can block tools
exp: For PreToolUse, exit code 2 is the blocking code, and stderr is shown to Claude. Other non-zero codes are non-blocking errors. A hook can also return structured JSON with permissionDecision 'deny' and a reason. PostToolUse runs after the tool has already executed.

q: A team wants Claude Code to keep working until the project's test suite passes, instead of declaring victory early when tests are still failing. Which deterministic mechanism supports this?
options: A Stop hook that runs the tests and, if they fail, blocks stopping with a reason so Claude continues working
A SessionStart hook that runs the tests once at the beginning of the session and stores the results
A line in CLAUDE.md asking Claude to never stop before all of the project's tests have been fixed
A PreToolUse hook on the Edit tool that runs the tests before every single file modification
exp: Stop hooks run when Claude finishes responding, and they can return a decision that blocks stopping, with a reason telling Claude what remains. That makes 'keep going until tests pass' deterministic. CLAUDE.md is only guidance.

q: An engineer is tired of approving every npm test invocation in Claude Code, but wants all other Bash commands to keep prompting. Which permissions configuration achieves this?
options: Add "Bash(npm run test:*)" to permissions.allow in the project or local settings file
Add "Bash(*)" to permissions.allow, then tell Claude in CLAUDE.md to only run the npm test commands
Start each session with --dangerously-skip-permissions so that test commands never trigger approval prompts
Add "npm test" to permissions.deny, since deny rules for a command make Claude run it without prompting
exp: Permission rules can target specific commands by prefix, such as Bash(npm run test:*), auto-approving only those while everything else follows normal prompting. Bash(*) or skipping permissions is far too broad, and deny rules block commands.

q: A developer wants to run two independent Claude Code sessions at the same time in one repository: one implementing a new feature and one fixing an unrelated bug, without the sessions' file changes interfering with each other. What is the recommended approach?
options: Create separate git worktrees for each task and run a Claude Code session in each worktree
Run both sessions in the same working directory, and ask each session to avoid touching the other's files
Use a single session and alternate between the tasks with /clear whenever the developer switches between them
Clone the repository to a new machine for the second task, since Claude Code allows only one session per machine
exp: Git worktrees give each session its own checkout of a separate branch while sharing repository history, so parallel sessions don't overwrite each other. A shared directory risks conflicts, and nothing limits sessions to one per machine.

q: An engineer uses a third-party MCP server in Claude Code whose query tool returns very large results, and Claude Code warns that the tool output exceeds its token limit. The engineer cannot change the server. What client-side adjustment raises the allowed size?
options: Set the MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS environment variable to a higher value before launching Claude Code
Run /compact before each query so that more context window space is available for the tool output
Add --max-tokens to the claude command, since that flag controls how large MCP tool outputs may be
Switch the server to stdio transport, since stdio servers have no limit on how much output they return
exp: Claude Code limits MCP tool output tokens by default and warns about large outputs. The MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS environment variable raises the limit on the client side. Server authors can also annotate tools to allow larger outputs. Transport type and /compact don't change this limit.

q: A team wants to run Claude Code fully autonomously overnight with --dangerously-skip-permissions to fix lint errors across a repository. What is the recommended safeguard?
options: Run it only inside an isolated container or VM without internet access and without production credentials
Run it on a developer's laptop, since the flag still prompts before deleting files or using the network
Run it on a production server, so it can verify fixes directly against live traffic during the night
Run it anywhere, since Claude Code automatically sandboxes every command when this flag is enabled
exp: Skipping permissions removes all approval prompts, so Anthropic recommends using it only in an isolated environment such as a container without internet access, to limit damage from mistakes or prompt injection. It provides no automatic protections.

q: A team wants to reduce how often Claude Code asks for permission when running Bash commands, while still preventing commands from reading files outside the project or reaching arbitrary hosts on the network. Which built-in feature is designed for this?
options: Enable Claude Code's sandboxed Bash, which enforces filesystem and network isolation so sandboxed commands can run with fewer prompts
Add Bash(*) to permissions.allow and rely on a CLAUDE.md instruction to stay inside the project directory
Switch to plan mode permanently, since plan mode executes Bash commands inside an isolated sandbox
Use the --verbose flag, which logs every command so that prompts are no longer needed for approval
exp: Claude Code's sandbox uses OS-level isolation to restrict filesystem access and network destinations for Bash commands. That lets more commands run autonomously, with fewer prompts, while keeping boundaries enforced. Allow-all rules plus instructions provide no enforcement.

q: An engineering team wants teammates to be able to mention @claude in a GitHub pull request comment and have Claude Code implement the requested change and push a commit to the PR branch. What is the most direct way to set this up?
options: Install the Claude GitHub app and the Claude Code GitHub Actions workflow, for example with /install-github-app
Add a webhook that emails the PR comment to an engineer who then runs Claude Code locally on the branch
Commit a CLAUDE.md to the repository, since Claude Code monitors GitHub comments in any repo that has one
Enable the web_search server tool on the repository so that Claude can read pull request comments online
exp: Claude Code GitHub Actions responds to @claude mentions in PRs and issues and can implement changes. The /install-github-app command guides setup of the app, workflow, and secrets. CLAUDE.md alone does not watch GitHub.

q: An MCP server marks its delete_records tool with destructiveHint: true and its list_records tool with readOnlyHint: true. A client developer plans to auto-approve every tool the server labels read-only. Which TWO statements about tool annotations are accurate? (Select TWO.)
options: Annotations are hints describing tool behavior, not security guarantees enforced by the protocol
Clients should not rely on annotations from untrusted servers when making permission or safety decisions
Annotations are cryptographically signed by the server, so a client can fully trust a readOnlyHint value
A tool marked readOnlyHint is blocked by the protocol from making any changes, so auto-approval is safe
exp: MCP tool annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) are advisory metadata. The spec says clients must treat them as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server. Nothing in the protocol enforces them or signs them.

q: A team builds an MCP server that needs an LLM to summarize long log files before returning results, but the server should not hold its own model API key; it should use the model available to the connected client, with the user retaining control. Which MCP capability fits?
options: Sampling, which lets the server request an LLM completion through the client
Resources, which let the server expose the log files as readable URIs
Prompts, which let the server register a reusable template for summarizing
Roots, which let the server learn which directories it is allowed to access
exp: Sampling lets a server ask the client to perform an LLM completion, so the server needs no API key and the client keeps human-in-the-loop control. Resources expose data, prompts are templates, and roots define filesystem boundaries.

q: A developer creates a Skill with frontmatter name "Contract Reviewer!" and a long description, and uploading it fails validation. What is the most likely cause?
options: The name must use only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens (for example contract-reviewer), within the length limit
The name must exactly match the name of a pre-built Anthropic Skill, since custom names are not allowed
Skills cannot include a description field; only the name is permitted in the SKILL.md frontmatter
The name must be written in all capital letters so that Claude can find it when scanning metadata
exp: Skill names have constraints: lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens, with a maximum length. Descriptions are required and also have a length limit. 'Contract Reviewer!' contains spaces, capitals, and punctuation.

q: A team's SKILL.md has grown to 2,000 lines covering five unrelated database dialects, and Claude's performance with the Skill has degraded. Following Anthropic's Skill authoring best practices, how should it be restructured?
options: Keep SKILL.md concise as an overview and move dialect-specific details into separate reference files it links to, loaded only when needed
Merge all five dialect sections into a single dense paragraph so the file has fewer lines but carries the same total information
Move the whole Skill content into the description field, since the description is always loaded and is never truncated
Duplicate the full SKILL.md into each bundled reference file so that Claude finds every detail no matter which file it opens
exp: Best practice is a concise SKILL.md body that acts like a table of contents, with detailed material split into separate files referenced one level deep. This uses progressive disclosure so only the relevant dialect gets loaded. Descriptions have a length limit and are meant for discovery.

q: A consumer chatbot has suffered jailbreak attempts in which users try to get it to produce policy-violating content. Which TWO mitigations are recommended in Anthropic's guidance on strengthening guardrails? (Select TWO.)
options: Pre-screen user inputs with a lightweight model such as Haiku acting as a harmlessness classifier
Continuously monitor outputs and flagged conversations, and iterate on prompts and safeguards
Rely on a single sentence in the system prompt that says "never comply with jailbreaks"
Raise the temperature so that the model's refusals are less predictable for attackers
exp: Anthropic suggests harmlessness screens using a lightweight model to classify inputs, input validation, ethical framing in the system prompt, and continuous monitoring with layered safeguards. A single instruction or sampling changes are not robust defenses.

q: A healthcare startup logs every full prompt and response for debugging, and these logs, which include patients' personal health information, are readable by the entire engineering organization. A privacy review flags this. Which change best addresses the risk while keeping useful debugging data?
options: Minimize and redact sensitive fields before logging, restrict log access to need-to-know roles, and apply retention limits
Keep logging everything, but add a system prompt instruction telling Claude not to include health information in its responses
Move the logs into a different folder of the same shared bucket, with a filename that indicates the logs contain sensitive data
Base64-encode the logged prompts and responses so that casual readers in the organization cannot read the health information
exp: Data minimization, redaction, least-privilege access, and retention limits are the standard controls for sensitive data in logs. Encoding is not protection, and prompt instructions do not cover the user inputs being logged.

q: A team migrated prompts written for an older model that used to under-use its tools. The prompts contain lines like "CRITICAL: You MUST ALWAYS use the search tool for EVERY question!" On a current Claude model, the agent now calls search even for trivial questions it can answer directly. What does Anthropic's guidance recommend?
options: Dial back the aggressive language to normal phrasing, since current models are more responsive to instructions and may overtrigger
Add more capitalized warnings about when not to use the tool, balancing out the emphasis on always using it
Set tool_choice to none on every request and remove search entirely, since the model cannot judge when to search
Lower the effort to the minimum so the model has less capacity to make tool calls on simple questions
exp: Current Claude models follow system prompts closely. Anthropic notes that emphatic language written to fix undertriggering in older models now causes overtriggering, and recommends calmer, normal phrasing, ideally with context on when a tool is useful.

q: A single huge prompt asks Claude to research a topic, analyze the findings, draft a report, and format it for publication. Errors keep appearing in the analysis step, and the team cannot tell which part of the prompt is responsible. What is the recommended restructuring?
options: Chain the work into separate prompts (research, analysis, drafting, formatting), passing outputs between them with XML tags
Add more detail to the single prompt so every step is described more thoroughly in one place for the model
Repeat the full prompt three times and keep the version of the report whose analysis looks most convincing
Move every instruction into the user message, since system prompts make multi-step tasks harder to follow
exp: Prompt chaining gives each subtask Claude's full attention and makes each step easy to inspect and debug on its own. Handing outputs between steps in XML tags keeps them clearly delimited.

q: A legal-tech application gives Claude a generic system prompt and gets contract risk analyses that are accurate but miss business implications a seasoned in-house lawyer would flag. Which prompt technique most directly targets this gap?
options: Use the system prompt to give Claude a specific role, such as general counsel of a fast-growing SaaS company, alongside the task context
Increase max_tokens so the model can write longer analyses that eventually cover business implications as well
Ask the user to rephrase each question more politely, since tone of the user message improves analytical depth
Remove the system prompt entirely so the model does not get confused by any framing before the contract text
exp: Role prompting through the system parameter is a powerful way to shift Claude's perspective and domain focus, for example toward legal and business implications. Length budgets and politeness do not change the perspective of the analysis.

q: A support team evaluates a ticket classifier that must output exactly one of twelve category labels, and they have thousands of labeled historical tickets. Which grading approach is most appropriate?
options: Code-based exact-match grading of the predicted label against the ground-truth label for every ticket
Human graders reading each predicted label and giving an overall impression score from 1 to 10
An LLM judge writing an essay critique of each classification that is then summarized by hand
Measuring the average length of the classifier's responses as a proxy for classification quality
exp: For outputs with a single correct answer, such as classification labels, code-based exact-match grading is the fastest, cheapest, and most reliable choice, and it scales to thousands of cases. Human or LLM grading fits open-ended outputs.

q: A team currently tests prompt changes by trying five handpicked examples and eyeballing the outputs. Before a high-stakes launch, they want a more trustworthy evaluation. Which TWO practices align with Anthropic's guidance on building evals? (Select TWO.)
options: Build a larger automated test set, favoring volume of test cases with automated grading over a few hand-graded ones
Make the test cases mirror the real-world task distribution, including edge cases and difficult or ambiguous inputs
Keep testing only the five examples that already pass, so the evaluation remains stable as the prompt changes
Grade outputs only by how confident and fluent they sound, since fluent responses are usually correct in practice
exp: Anthropic advises task-specific evals that reflect the real distribution, including edge cases, and prioritizing more questions with automated grading over fewer hand-graded ones. Fluency is not correctness, and a fixed set of already-passing examples hides regressions.
